Itraconazole (Abuhelwa 2015)

Source: vignettes/articles/Abuhelwa_2015_itraconazole.Rmd
Abuhelwa_2015_itraconazole.Rmd

Model and source 

mod  <- readModelDb("Abuhelwa_2015_itraconazole")
meta <- rxode2::rxode(mod)
#> ℹ parameter labels from comments will be replaced by 'label()'
  • Citation: Abuhelwa AY, Foster DJR, Mudge S, Hayes D, Upton RN. Population pharmacokinetic modeling of itraconazole and hydroxyitraconazole for oral SUBA-itraconazole and Sporanox capsule formulations in healthy subjects in fed and fasted states. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2015;59(9):5681-5696. doi:10.1128/AAC.00973-15.
  • Description: Population PK model for oral itraconazole and its active metabolite hydroxy-itraconazole in healthy adults (Abuhelwa 2015). Two-compartment parent with 4-transit-compartment Savic-style absorption and a one-compartment hydroxy-itraconazole metabolite eliminated by mixed linear and Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Encodes the SUBA-itraconazole vs Sporanox formulation effect on relative bioavailability (with formulation-dependent scaling of the F variability) and the fed-vs-fasted effect on both relative bioavailability and the transit-absorption rate constant; the metabolic conversion ratio fm is assumed = 1 so all parent clearance becomes metabolite, and the metabolite CL/V are apparent values scaled by the unknown fm.
  • Article: Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2015;59(9):5681-5696
  • Supplement (NONMEM control streams for the final itraconazole and metabolite models): AAC.00973-15 supplemental material

Population

The model was fit to pooled phase I crossover bioequivalence data from seven Mayne Pharma International trials comparing SUBA-itraconazole (a solid dispersion of itraconazole in a pH-dependent polymeric matrix marketed as Lozanoc / Itragerm) with Sporanox (Janssen Pharmaceuticals capsule reference product). Five studies were conducted in the United States and two in the United Kingdom (Abuhelwa 2015 Table 1). Overall, 238 healthy adult subjects contributed 15,097 itraconazole and 9,868 hydroxy-itraconazole plasma concentrations across 2-4 treatment periods per subject. Subjects were non-tobacco-using, non-pregnant non-lactating adults aged 18-60 years (median ~ 35 y); weight ranged 49-108 kg; the cohort was ~ 61% female and ~ 76% White, with ~ 11% Black, < 1% Asian, and ~ 13% Other (Abuhelwa 2015 Table 2). Subjects with histories of gastrointestinal disease, malabsorption, or recent CYP3A inhibitor / inducer exposure were excluded.

meta$population
#> $species
#> [1] "human"

Source trace

The per-parameter origin is recorded as an in-file comment next to each ini() entry in inst/modeldb/specificDrugs/Abuhelwa_2015_itraconazole.R. The table below collects them in one place for review.

Virtual cohort

Original observed plasma concentration data are not publicly available. The simulations below use virtual cohorts whose covariate distributions (formulation, fed state) match the published bioequivalence simulation scenarios in Abuhelwa 2015 Table 5 (single oral doses of bioequivalent strengths: 100 mg Sporanox and 58 mg SUBA-itraconazole in fed and fasted periods). The seed is fixed for reproducibility.

set.seed(2015)

n_per_arm <- 100L
sim_horizon_h <- 72

# Build one bioequivalence-comparison arm.
make_arm <- function(n, dose_mg, fed, form_suba, id_offset = 0L) {
  obs_grid <- c(seq(0.1, 8, by = 0.2), seq(8.5, sim_horizon_h, by = 0.5))
  base <- tibble(
    id        = id_offset + seq_len(n),
    FED       = as.integer(fed),
    FORM_ITR_SUBA = as.integer(form_suba),
    amt       = dose_mg
  )
  doses <- base |>
    mutate(time = 0, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot")
  obs <- base |>
    select(id, FED, FORM_ITR_SUBA) |>
    tidyr::crossing(time = obs_grid) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L, cmt = "Cc", amt = NA_real_)
  bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid)) |>
    mutate(
      formulation = ifelse(FORM_ITR_SUBA == 1L, "SUBA-itraconazole", "Sporanox"),
      fed_status  = ifelse(FED == 1L, "Fed", "Fasted"),
      treatment   = paste0(formulation, " - ", fed_status)
    )
}

events <- bind_rows(
  make_arm(n_per_arm, dose_mg = 100, fed = 0L, form_suba = 0L, id_offset = 0L),
  make_arm(n_per_arm, dose_mg = 100, fed = 1L, form_suba = 0L, id_offset = 1L * n_per_arm),
  make_arm(n_per_arm, dose_mg =  58, fed = 0L, form_suba = 1L, id_offset = 2L * n_per_arm),
  make_arm(n_per_arm, dose_mg =  58, fed = 1L, form_suba = 1L, id_offset = 3L * n_per_arm)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unique(events[, c("id", "time", "evid")])))

Simulation

The stochastic simulation draws between-subject random effects from the published variance components.

sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  object     = mod,
  events     = events,
  keep       = c("FED", "FORM_ITR_SUBA", "formulation", "fed_status", "treatment"),
  returnType = "data.frame"
) |>
  filter(time > 0)
#> ℹ parameter labels from comments will be replaced by 'label()'

For deterministic typical-value replication (used to overlay the published geometric-mean trajectories below), zero out the between-subject random effects.

sim_typ <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  object     = rxode2::zeroRe(mod),
  events     = events,
  keep       = c("FED", "FORM_ITR_SUBA", "formulation", "fed_status", "treatment"),
  returnType = "data.frame"
) |>
  filter(time > 0)
#> ℹ parameter labels from comments will be replaced by 'label()'
#> ℹ omega/sigma items treated as zero: 'etalcl', 'etalvc', 'etalktr', 'etafvar', 'etalcl_ohi'
#> Warning: multi-subject simulation without without 'omega'

Replicate published figures

Food effect on itraconazole concentrations (Abuhelwa 2015 Figure 7)

Figure 7 of Abuhelwa 2015 plots the predicted itraconazole concentration vs time for bioequivalent oral doses of Sporanox (100 mg) and SUBA-itraconazole (58 mg) in the fed and fasted states. The figure below reproduces the typical-value time course for the same dose pairs, separating parent and metabolite. Fed status shifts the parent Tmax later (slower transit-compartment absorption) and lowers Cmax (lower bioavailability and slower KTR), independent of formulation - the central observation of the food-effect simulation in the source paper.

sim_typ_one <- sim_typ |>
  group_by(formulation, fed_status, time) |>
  slice_head(n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

sim_typ_long <- sim_typ_one |>
  pivot_longer(c(Cc, Cc_ohi), names_to = "analyte", values_to = "conc") |>
  mutate(analyte = recode(analyte,
                          Cc     = "Itraconazole",
                          Cc_ohi = "Hydroxy-itraconazole"))

ggplot(sim_typ_long, aes(time, conc, colour = fed_status)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid(analyte ~ formulation, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 48)) +
  labs(x = "Time after dose (h)",
       y = "Plasma concentration (ng/mL)",
       colour = "Fed state",
       title = "Typical-value profiles for bioequivalent doses",
       caption = paste0(
         "Replicates Figure 7 of Abuhelwa 2015 (typical-value version): ",
         "100 mg Sporanox and 58 mg SUBA-itraconazole, fed vs fasted."
       )) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
#> Warning: Removed 384 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_line()`).

Stochastic VPC of itraconazole (Abuhelwa 2015 Figure 5 – single-dose stratified)

Figure 5 of Abuhelwa 2015 shows the visual predictive check of itraconazole for single-dose studies stratified by fed status and formulation. The figure below replicates the stratified VPC band using the simulated cohort above.

vpc <- sim |>
  group_by(formulation, fed_status, time) |>
  summarise(
    Q05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q50 = quantile(Cc, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(vpc, aes(time, Q50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95, fill = fed_status), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = fed_status), linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ formulation) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 48)) +
  labs(x = "Time after dose (h)",
       y = "Itraconazole (ng/mL)",
       colour = "Fed state",
       fill   = "Fed state",
       title  = "Single-dose stratified VPC: itraconazole",
       caption = paste0(
         "Replicates Figure 5 of Abuhelwa 2015 (single-dose stratified VPC): ",
         "ribbons span the 5th-95th percentile of simulated subjects."
       )) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
#> Warning: Removed 192 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_ribbon()`).
#> Warning: Removed 192 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_line()`).

PKNCA validation

We run PKNCA on the stochastic simulation and compare the per-arm geometric means with Abuhelwa 2015 Table 5 (model-predicted food effects for bioequivalent Sporanox 100 mg and SUBA-itraconazole 58 mg).

sim_nca <- sim |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc), time > 0) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, treatment)

dose_df <- events |>
  filter(evid == 1L) |>
  select(id, time, amt, treatment)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | treatment + id,
                             concu = "ng/mL", timeu = "hr")
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id,
                             doseu = "mg")

intervals <- data.frame(
  start       = 0,
  end         = Inf,
  cmax        = TRUE,
  tmax        = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs  = TRUE,
  half.life   = TRUE
)

nca_data <- PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals)
nca_res  <- PKNCA::pk.nca(nca_data)

per_id <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result)
per_id_wide <- per_id |>
  select(treatment, id, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)

# Geometric mean helper (drops non-positive values for cmax/auc).
gmean <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x) & x > 0]
  if (length(x) == 0) NA_real_ else exp(mean(log(x)))
}

summary_tbl <- per_id_wide |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(
    Cmax_geomean      = gmean(cmax),
    Tmax_median       = stats::median(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    AUCinf_geomean    = gmean(aucinf.obs),
    halflife_median   = stats::median(half.life, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_subjects        = sum(!is.na(cmax)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
knitr::kable(summary_tbl,
             digits = 2,
             caption = "Simulated itraconazole NCA parameters by treatment arm (geometric means / medians).")

Comparison against Abuhelwa 2015 Table 5

The published Table 5 reports geometric means (90 % CI) for the bioequivalent dose pair. The simulated values from the stochastic cohort above are side-by-side with the source. Differences below ~ 20 % are expected because (i) the published Table 5 uses 1,000 simulations of 52 subjects each from a crossover design while the present cohort uses 400 subjects in a parallel-arm design, and (ii) the typical-value replication is sensitive to the precise way log-normal random effects on F, KTR, and CL combine into a non-linear Cmax / Tmax statistic.

published_table5 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~treatment,                       ~Cmax_pub, ~Tmax_pub, ~AUCinf_pub,
  "Sporanox - Fasted",                 78.31,      3.86,      831.52,
  "Sporanox - Fed",                    51.37,      6.83,      675.39,
  "SUBA-itraconazole - Fasted",        81.18,      3.87,      833.52,
  "SUBA-itraconazole - Fed",           50.23,      6.83,      653.60
)

comparison <- summary_tbl |>
  select(treatment, Cmax_geomean, Tmax_median, AUCinf_geomean) |>
  left_join(published_table5, by = "treatment") |>
  mutate(
    Cmax_pct    = 100 * (Cmax_geomean   - Cmax_pub)   / Cmax_pub,
    Tmax_pct    = 100 * (Tmax_median    - Tmax_pub)   / Tmax_pub,
    AUCinf_pct  = 100 * (AUCinf_geomean - AUCinf_pub) / AUCinf_pub
  )

knitr::kable(comparison,
             digits = c(0, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1),
             caption = "Simulated geometric means vs Abuhelwa 2015 Table 5 (signed % difference relative to the published value).")
Simulated geometric means vs Abuhelwa 2015 Table 5 (signed % difference relative to the published value).

Assumptions and deviations

  • Multidose mechanics not implemented. The published model adds two empirical multidose corrections that were retained in the final fit because they improved the description of the day-15 multidose data in studies 705 (100 mg / 200 mg q.d.) and 706 (200 mg / 400 mg b.i.d.): a daily-dose- and time-dependent decrease in clearance, DDCL = (1 - DDCLss) * exp(-Kss * (DAY - 1)) + DDCLss with DDCLss = exp(-DDK * EDD) and DDK = 0.0065 (Sporanox) / 0.00596 (SUBA-itraconazole), and a similar time-dependent increase in bioavailability with DDFss = 3.26 (Abuhelwa 2015 Eq. 5-7 and Table 3 rows DDKSPOR / DDKSUBA / DDmax / DDFss). The metabolite model also has a per-multidose-study TIMECLM correction (CL_m,M5 = (1 + (-0.208)) * CL_m,SD for study 10850705 q.d. and CL_m,M6 = (1 + (-0.643)) * CL_m,SD for study 10850706 b.i.d.; Abuhelwa 2015 Table 4 CLM5 / CLM6 and Eq. 8) and the Michaelis-Menten metabolite-elimination term is turned off in the multidose studies. These corrections are tightly coupled to the specific Mayne Pharma trials in the source dataset and are not implemented in this extraction. Single-dose simulations from the present model degenerate cleanly to the paper’s single-dose typical-value behaviour (DAY = 1 implies DDCL = DDF = 1). Users wishing to reproduce the published multidose VPCs should either extend the model with these terms or fit them locally.

  • Study-population (US vs UK) effect not implemented. Abuhelwa 2015 identifies a study-population covariate (collinear with the Sporanox source country) with a -16.6 % effect on apparent CL/F and a +33.8 % effect on KTR (Table 3 rows STUDYPOP-CL/F and STUDYPOP-KTR; supplement THETA(20)/(21) and SPORORG input column). The effect was retained in the final covariate model but was discussed by the authors as not clinically interpretable (the most likely explanation, gastric-pH or gut-transit differences across the trial centres, is not directly observable). The present model treats the US studies as the structural reference; users who need the UK-study scaling can multiply the parent CL/F by 0.834 and KTR by 1.338 inside model() (or apply the same factors to the simulated outputs post-hoc) without re-fitting.

  • V_max unit label. Abuhelwa 2015 Table 4 labels the V_max units as “liters/h”, but the supplement Appendix S1 NONMEM control stream header states “;UNITS ARE UG, L (NG/ML) AND H” and Appendix S2 implements the Michaelis-Menten flux as (VMAX * C8) / (KM + C8) in the metabolite ODE (Appendix S2 page 17). With internal amounts in micrograms and concentrations in ng/mL (= ug/L), the V_max value 403 must be in mass/time units (micrograms per hour) for the flux term to be in micrograms per hour. The model file therefore treats V_max = 403 ug/h and the Table 4 unit label is interpreted as a presentation error.

  • LTBS combined residual error mapped to nlmixr2 add + prop in linear space. The source uses a log-transform-both-sides residual error model (Methods Eq. 2 and supplement Appendix S1 W = sqrt(THETA_prop^2 + THETA_add^2 / exp(IPRE)^2) ; Y = IPRE + W * EPS(1) with EPS(1) SD fixed to 1 in $SIGMA). This is equivalent in linear space to Cc ~ add(addSd) + prop(propSd) for the concentration magnitudes used in the trial; the parameter labels and numerical values map directly onto Abuhelwa 2015 Table 3 and Table 4.

  • Residual error: single-dose fasted set used for the parent. The source reports separate residual-error magnitudes for single-dose fasted (propSd = 0.293, addSd = 0.168 ng/mL), single-dose fed (propSd = 0.399, addSd = 0.140 ng/mL), and multidose (propSd = 0.141, addSd = 0.267 ng/mL) parent observations (Abuhelwa 2015 Table 3 RV section). This model uses the single-dose fasted values as the structural default because (i) the primary bioequivalence-simulation scenario in the source paper is fasted single dose, and (ii) the multidose residual-error values are only meaningful when paired with the multidose DDCL / DDF mechanics which are not implemented here. Users simulating fed or multidose scenarios who need the precise published residual SDs can override propSd / addSd via rxode2::ini() on the loaded model.

  • Common variability on bioavailability (FVAR) declared as a paper-specific eta. The shared random effect on F (Abuhelwa 2015 stage 1: “common variability on bioavailability” approach with FVAR magnitude 56.4 % CV) has no matching fixed-effect typical-value parameter (the typical value is 1 by construction). The model file declares etafvar via the paper_specific_etas metadata field so checkModelConventions() does not flag the missing matching fvar parameter.

  • Dose-unit internal conversion (f(depot) <- fbio * 1000). Abuhelwa 2015 reports apparent oral CL/F and V/F in L/h and L (i.e. amounts in mg, volumes in L, concentrations in ng/mL = ug/L), but the supplement Appendix S1 / S2 NONMEM control stream states “;UNITS ARE UG, L (NG/ML) AND H”

    • i.e. internal amounts in micrograms. The model file accepts the user-facing oral dose in mg and converts it to internal micrograms by multiplying the depot bioavailability by 1000. This keeps the Michaelis-Menten V_max in ug/h dimensionally consistent with the linear elimination flux (cl_ohi / vc_ohi) * central_ohi (also in ug/h when central_ohi is in ug) without requiring users to dose in non-standard units.

  • Cohort design – parallel arms, not crossover. The cohort simulated for the PKNCA validation uses 200 subjects per arm in a parallel-arm design rather than the crossover design used by the source paper’s 1,000-replicate bioequivalence simulations. Per-arm geometric means are stable for the comparison against Abuhelwa 2015 Table 5 but per-arm CIs are wider than the source’s crossover CIs because they do not benefit from the within-subject variance cancellation. This is a vignette-level simulation convenience, not a model deviation.
